title: Pool vs Snooker vs Carom: What's the Difference? A Beginner's Guide
description: Pool, snooker and carom billiards look alike but play very differently. Compare tables, pockets, balls and rules in one easy cheat sheet.
body:
You flip past a TV channel and see a giant green table, tiny pockets and a rainbow of balls. Is it pool? Not quite. Pool, snooker and carom billiards all use cues and cloth, but they are three very different games. Here is a friendly guide so you can tell them apart in seconds.

The quick answer

Pool has pockets and 15 numbered balls. Snooker has a much bigger table, tighter pockets and 22 balls. Carom has no pockets at all. If you see a table with no holes, you are watching carom.

Pool: the one you know from the bar

Pool is the most popular cue sport in the United States. A pro table is 9 by 4.5 feet, and home and bar tables are often 7 or 8 feet. It has six pockets and 16 balls: the white cue ball plus 15 numbered object balls, each 2.25 inches across.

Popular pool games include 8-ball, 9-ball, 10-ball and straight pool. In 9-ball you must always hit the lowest-numbered ball first, and the player who pockets the 9 wins. Curious about the differences? Read our 8-ball vs 9-ball vs 10-ball guide. Events like the Mosconi Cup are played with 9-ball rules.

Snooker: bigger table, smaller balls

Snooker is hugely popular in the United Kingdom and across Asia. The full-size table is 12 by 6 feet, and the balls are smaller, about 52.5 mm across (roughly 2 1/16 inches). The pockets are also tighter, with rounded openings, so precision matters more than power.

The set has 22 balls: 15 reds, six colored balls (yellow, green, brown, blue, pink and black) and one white cue ball. Players score points by pocketing balls with set values, and they pocket a red before a color. Fouls give points to the opponent. Break-building is the big thrill: long runs of reds and colors in a row.

Carom: no pockets, all angles

Carom billiards, including popular three-cushion billiards, has no pockets. The table is bounded entirely by cushions. Many amateur tables measure about 10 by 5 feet, and the international standard playing surface is about 2.84 by 1.42 meters (112 by 56 inches).

There are only three balls: two cue balls (one white, one yellow) and one red ball. Each player shoots a cue ball and tries to make it contact both other balls. In three-cushion, your ball must also touch the cushions at least three times before it hits the second ball. A successful shot scores one point, and a miss costs nothing. Carom balls are larger than pool balls, about 61.5 mm.

Side-by-side cheat sheet

  • Table: pool 9 ft pro size, snooker 12 ft, carom often about 10 ft.
  • Pockets: pool 6, snooker 6 (tight), carom none.
  • Balls: pool 16, snooker 22, carom 3.
  • Ball size: snooker about 52.5 mm, pool 57.15 mm, carom about 61.5 mm.
  • How you win: pool, pocket your balls (and the 8 or 9); snooker, score more points; carom, make more scoring shots.

Which one should you try first?

If you are brand new, start with pool. Tables are easy to find, the rules are simple and you can learn the basics quickly. Our pool guides walk you through the stance, the bridge and aiming, and our table sizes explainer helps you choose a table. If you want to know the lingo, check the pool terms glossary.

Snooker and carom are wonderful once you are comfortable with cue control. Many top pool players say that learning other games sharpens their skills, because snooker teaches patience and carom teaches angles and speed.

How each game feels to play

Pool rewards a mix of power and planning. You break the rack, pick your shots and think about where the cue ball will stop for the next one. That is called position play, and you can learn more in our cue ball control guide.

Snooker is more like chess on felt. Because the table is long and the pockets are tight, players often play safeties, which means leaving the cue ball where the opponent cannot easily score. A single frame can last a long time, and a big break can swing it in minutes.

Carom is a game of geometry. With no pockets to aim at, you read how the balls will bounce off the cushions and how spin changes the angle. It looks effortless when experts do it, and it is very hard to master.

No matter which one you pick, a few habits help everywhere: a steady stance, a smooth stroke and a calm pre-shot routine. Our pre-shot routine guide works for all three.

Where to watch pool this week

The biggest pool event of the year is almost here: the Mosconi Cup runs November 27 to 30 at the Caribe Royale in Orlando, Florida, with Team USA facing Team Europe. Sessions start at 1 p.m. ET, and ESPN+ is reported to carry all four days in the United States. Check our Mosconi Cup 2026 hub for updates and see big tournaments for what is next.

So, the next time somebody calls every cue sport "pool," you can smile and tell them the difference.
